sections.html:
Harlan County lies in southeastern Kentucky against the Virginia line. Harlan is the county seat and Cumberland is the largest city. Coal built the economy, and the population has fallen with it, from 26,831 in 2020 to an estimated 24,725 in July 2025. A seller here is entering a market that has shrunk for decades. That affects the sale price more than it affects the tax bill, but it decides how much cushion a house has when unpaid taxes or repairs come out of the proceeds.

The typical owned home is valued at $73,700. Owners live in 71.6 percent of the housing, and typical rent is $678 a month. The county has 13,136 housing units against 10,731 households, about 2,400 more units than households, and no building permits were recorded for 2025. On a house this size the yearly tax bill is small in dollars. The real risk is a string of unpaid years in which interest and fees grow faster than the home's value.

Each office keeps its own schedule, so call before you drive in.

  • Sheriff: collects the bill. The sheriff's website links to an online public tax lookup. Call for the discount and penalty dates printed on your bill.
  • Property Valuation Administrator: write to P.O. Box 209 in Harlan (ZIP 40831) or call (606) 573-1990 between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.
  • County Clerk: phone (606) 573-3636. Monday it stays open until 6 p.m., Tuesday through Friday it closes at 4:30, and on the last Saturday of the month, holiday weekends excepted, it opens 9 a.m. to noon.

The clerk's website has a delinquent taxes page and a third-party purchaser application. The PVA's website carries the tax roll and a property search showing assessments and owners.

The PVA's website posts the state's cycle in a single chart.

How the Kentucky tax year runs for real estate
StepWhen
Assessment dateJanuary 1
Listing periodJanuary 1 through March 1
Tax roll open for review, conferences with the PVA13 days beginning on the first Monday of May
Appeals board hearingsFive days, beginning 25 to 35 days after review closes
Bills delivered to the sheriffNo later than September 15
Discount paymentsBy November 1
Payments at face valueNovember 2 through December 31
Bills turn delinquentJanuary 1, with 5 percent through January 31
10 percent penalty and 10 percent sheriff add-onAfter January 31
Sheriff passes bills to clerkApril 15
Clerk's certificate salesJuly 14 through August 28

A state-ordered delay can move a county to a slower plan with 30 days for each stage, so the dates on your own bill control.

Start with the PVA. A conference in the May inspection window is mandatory, and when it produces agreement the new value flows into the fall bill.

Without agreement you have until one workday after the window shuts to file at the clerk's office. A three-member local board, appointed by the largest city's mayor, the fiscal court and the county judge executive, meets about five weeks after inspection. It must reject a claim that comes with no facts, so gather sales of similar houses and repair estimates beforehand.

At these values an appeal pays off mostly when the PVA's record is wrong about something concrete, such as a bedroom count, a shed that no longer exists, or a fire-damaged building still carried at full value.

sections.h2: Does the buyer get the bill after closing?
sections.html:
Not automatically. The bill for a year goes to the January 1 owner, so a later sale leaves it in the seller's name for that year. PVA staff read the recorded deed and mail the bill to the new owner when they can. A buyer without a copy should call the sheriff.

List a mailing address the buyer will check in the deed, since the clerk cannot take a deed without an in-care-of address for that year's bill. A seller on the homestead exemption should also tell the PVA, since the exemption does not go to the buyer.

A bill still open when April 15 closes passes to the County Clerk, and a monthly 1 percent interest charge starts. On transfer the amount owed already includes the penalty, the sheriff add-on and an assumed commission. It climbs again within five business days, after the county attorney's first notice, and after the June advertisement.

Notices come by mail, and installment plans can be requested before a certificate is sold. If a third party buys it, the owner pays that buyer, who can add substantial fees.

An owner with unpaid years can still sell. The closing agent gets the payoff from the clerk and pays it from the proceeds. A cash offer on an older house can be weighed against a listing by comparing what is left after the payoff.

Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, and who live in the home can file for the exemption with the PVA under KRS 132.810. An owner under 65 qualifies only with a total disability. The exemption does not pass to a buyer, so report the sale to the PVA.

Ask the PVA for the current dollar figure and for the papers that prove age or disability. Because home values here are low, the saving is modest in dollars, but it is worth claiming every year you qualify.

Start by learning where each unpaid year sits. The sheriff's online lookup shows the current bill, and the clerk's delinquent taxes page covers anything that passed to the clerk after April 15. Then ask the clerk for a written payoff dated close to the closing day, since interest adds up monthly.

The title company will find any unpaid year, so there is no way to sell around it. What you can control is the timing. A bill paid before April 15 avoids the clerk's fees entirely. A bill already at the clerk should be cleared before certificate sales begin in July, because a third-party buyer who purchases the certificate adds charges and you then deal with that buyer instead of the county.

With low home values, a large payoff can eat much of the sale price. Compare what is left after the payoff on a listing with what a cash offer would leave, and weigh how long each route takes.

sections.h2: Buying near the parks and forest
sections.html: Part of Cumberland Gap National Historical Park and the Blanton Forest preserve lie in the county, so a house near them may draw outdoor-minded buyers. School district boundaries, city limits and fire protection can change the taxes on a bill, so ask the sheriff which districts appear on yours.

faqs.q: What is the last day for the Harlan County discount?
faqs.a: November 1. After that, the chart lists face value through the end of December and a 5 percent penalty in January.

faqs.q: How much extra does a February payment cost in Harlan County?
faqs.a: Ten percent in penalty plus a 10 percent sheriff add-on, both of which start once January ends. The state describes the total as 21 percent.

faqs.q: Who answers questions about my Harlan County assessed value?
faqs.a: The PVA at (606) 573-1990 handles the conference that must come before any appeal.

faqs.q: Where do I check for delinquent Harlan County taxes?
faqs.a: The County Clerk's website has a delinquent taxes page, and the clerk's office answers at (606) 573-3636. The sheriff hands over bills after April 15.

faqs.q: Can a Harlan County owner under 65 get the homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Yes, if totally disabled. KRS 132.810 opens the exemption to age 65 and up, or total disability, for owners living in the home, filed with the PVA.
